correctness.rationale: For three candidates, a transitive majority tournament has its Condorcet winner as unique Kemeny winner, while in a cycle the unique Kemeny winner is the candidate reached by breaking the unique weakest majority edge. Odd electorate size makes all nonzero majority margins odd, so a strict inequality between positive margins has gap at least two. One ballot can alter each pair margin by at most two, and a voter already sincerely preferring the target cannot improve the target's pairwise margin against the old winner. The case split in the proof therefore prevents the target edge from becoming uniquely weakest or flipping enough to make the target Condorcet winner. A fresh independent exhaustive replay through eleven voters checked 140,610 unilateral singleton-endpoint comparisons, including 16,572 singleton-to-singleton winner changes, and found zero profitable such changes.
risks: The result is not strategyproofness: tie resolution can create manipulation, and coalitions or four-plus candidates are outside scope.

originality.rationale: Wang--Cuff--Kulkarni give the closest prior classification: for three candidates, Kemeny strategic voting occurs only at boundaries separating winning rankings at Kendall distance two. Their full paper does not impose the odd-electorate parity lattice or state that a profitable one-ballot move cannot have singleton Kemeny-winner correspondences at both endpoints. The audited theorem is a parity-sensitive localization refinement, not the broad claim that Kemeny has no manipulation. Resultary found no equivalent singleton-to-singleton theorem.
residual_risks: The singleton-endpoint theorem may be derivable as an unrecorded corollary of the Wang boundary table; no such formulation was found.

evidence: Analytic all-odd-electorate theorem with a clear tie-localization consequence.
Finite replay confirms many singleton-to-singleton changes exist, so the exclusion is specifically about profitable changes rather than vacuity.
value.rationale: The result sharply localizes where three-candidate Kemeny manipulability can occur under the common odd-electorate setting: profitable unilateral moves cannot connect two unambiguous winner regions directly. This is a structural boundary statement that complements, rather than repeats, the prior continuous boundary classification.
risks: Its practical force depends on how a resolute implementation treats Kemeny ties.

final_claim: With exactly three candidates and an odd number of strict-ballot voters, a unilateral Kemeny manipulation cannot move from one singleton Kemeny winner to a sincerely preferred singleton Kemeny winner; any profitable resolute manipulation must touch an underlying Kemeny tie at one endpoint.
limitations: Exactly three candidates and odd electorate.
